newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss bankers say secrecy ease only for WW2 accounts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss bankers say secrecy ease only for WW2 accounts.

text.p: Switzerland's decision to relax its vaunted banking secrecy to search for Holocaust victims' dormant wealth affects only a limited number of wartime bank accounts and is irrelevant for modern clients, bankers said Friday.
They rejected what they referred to as rumours in foreign exchange markets that banking secrecy itself on a broad scale was in danger.

The Swiss franc dropped to 15-month lows against the German mark as markets reacted to a media report repeating the Swiss government's request to parliament to suspend a three-month waiting period for voters to object to new laws. If parliament approves the request, Switzerland's strict laws on banking secrecy could ease as early as December or Jan. 1 instead of April 1997.
The mark jumped from around 82.95 Swiss centimes to 83.70 late on Thursday and at midday in Europe on Friday, the mark was up another notch to 83.80 against the Swiss franc.
"Banking secrecy, let's keep that very clear, will not be lifted for the vast majority of foreign and even local Swiss clients," said Swiss Bank Corp.'s Janwillem Acket.
"Banking secrecy is a fundamental fact which will remain as solid as our vaults," he said. "This is not going to be changed. This is a fundamental asset of Switzerland as a financial centre."
Swiss banks deny allegations by Jewish groups and the head of the U.S. Senate Banking Committee that they are sitting on huge wealth left unclaimed by Jews murdered by the Nazis.

To help clear up the matter, parliament is set to give final approval in December to creating a panel of historians and experts empowered to lift banking secrecy in certain cases to help conduct a sweeping review of Switzerland's wartime role.
"The secrecy laws are going to be lifted only in cases where it is simply necesary to bring light into the dark of secrecy concerning the Holocaust victims' assets," Acket said.
"It is not going to touch any clients of the Swiss financial marketplace at all," he said. "This is only a small, minute detail which does not concern the normal Swiss bank client."
